rows.selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so we have zero information about which design choices (modality, profile setting, encoder, aggregation, fusion) actually matter or whether added complexity over a simple baseline provides any benefit. The most critical unknown is the performance floor of the simplest viable model. 2) What this tests: config_009 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the cleanest, most interpretable baseline—standard PCA on RNA with a single profile and no image modality, aggregation, or fusion. It establishes a reference performance level against which every more complex configuration (multimodal, multiprofile, learned encoders) must be compared to justify its added cost. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Under a limited budget, the single most informative first step is to anchor the search with a simple, fast, well-understood baseline. If config_009 performs well, all subsequent multimodal/multiprofile experiments must clearly beat it to be justified, sharply reducing the effective search space. If it performs poorly, we immediately know we must explore image or learned-encoder paths. Either outcome dramatically reduces uncertainty about the most important design axis (does RNA alone suffice?) and guides every subsequent experiment more efficiently than jumping into a complex multimodal configuration whose failure would be hard to attribute.

With only one completed experiment (config_009: RNA-only, PCA-2000, single profile, ~48.5% acc), the most critical uncertainty is whether adding image data provides any signal at all in this multimodal cellular profiling task. config_008 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, no aggregation, concat fusion) directly tests this by keeping the RNA encoder (pca_n2000) and profile setting (singleprofile) identical to the baseline, while introducing the minimal set of new variables required to add an image modality (ResNet50 + simple concat). This isolates the effect of modality/fusion as much as possible without confounding with encoder choice or profile complexity. If it substantially outperforms 48.5%, we know images carry complementary signal and can then explore better encoders/fusion. If it does not, we can redirect budget toward RNA encoder improvements or multiprofile settings. Testing an image-only baseline first would be informative but delays the practically central question of whether the multimodal combination works, and testing a more complex multimodal config (e.g., multiprofile + transformer aggregation) would confound too many variables with only one reference point.

Evidence: config_008 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) achieved 0.527 acc / 0.510 F1, a clear +4.2% improvement over the RNA-only baseline (config_009, 0.485 acc). This confirms that the pca_n2000 + resnet50 + concat combination is a strong foundation. Uncertainty: We have no evidence yet on whether multiprofile aggregation adds value beyond the single-profile setting. This experiment (config_003) tests exactly that question by switching from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation while holding the RNA encoder (pca_n2000), image encoder (resnet50), and fusion (concat) identical to config_008. This is the cleanest possible comparison to isolate the effect of multiprofile + avgpool, changing only the profile/aggregation axis. Under a limited budget, confirming or ruling out the multiprofile benefit on top of the already-validated multimodal pipeline is the highest-information next step before investing in more complex variations (different encoders, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion).

Evidence: config_003 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) achieved 0.619 acc, a large +9.2% jump over config_008 (same but singleprofile, no aggregation at 0.527). This shows multiprofile + avgpool is the dominant driver so far. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether avgpool is the optimal aggregation or whether a transformer aggregation would further improve multiprofile integration. Question tested: config_014 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding all other settings identical to config_003 (pca_n2000, resnet50, concat, multiprofile), cleanly isolating the aggregation effect. Why this is the best next experiment: aggregation is the most recently introduced and highest-impact design axis; resolving whether a more expressive aggregator (transformer) helps or whether simple averaging already captures the multiprofile benefit will either open a new high-performing direction or confirm we should focus remaining budget on image encoder or fusion method. A single-variable comparison with the current best is the most information-efficient use of the next slot.

The current best (config_003: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat; acc 0.619) uses PCA—a linear, untrained dimensionality reduction—as the RNA encoder. The only other dimension we've tested is aggregation (avgpool > transformer), while the RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion strategy remain unexplored. Config_011 changes exactly one variable (RNA encoder: pca_n2000 → scvi_n200) while holding everything else fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, concat), giving a clean single-factor comparison. This tests whether a nonlinear, learned RNA representation (scVI) captures structure that PCA misses, which is a fundamental design decision for cellular profiling. If scvi_n200 significantly outperforms PCA, it signals that representation quality on the RNA side is a major lever and justifies further exploration (e.g., scgpt). If it does not, PCA is sufficient and we can redirect budget toward image-encoder or fusion questions. Under a limited budget, isolating the RNA-encoder effect is the highest-information next step because it addresses the most basic representational assumption in the current best model.

Evidence: The current best (config_011, acc 0.632) uses scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + concat in a multimodal multiprofile setup. We know multimodal helps (+4% over rna_only) and multiprofile helps substantially (+9% over singleprofile), but all experiments so far have used resnet50 as the image encoder. Uncertainty: We have zero evidence on whether a stronger image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) would further improve performance, which is a representation-level question with potentially large impact. This experiment (config_020: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) is a clean single-variable change from config_011, isolating the image encoder effect. It is the best next experiment because the image representation quality is a more fundamental and potentially higher-impact design axis than fusion mechanism (concat vs weighted), and resolving whether the image modality can contribute more signal directly informs whether to invest further in image-side design choices.

The current best configuration (config_020: scvi_n200, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) achieves 0.715 accuracy, and the largest single gain came from upgrading the image encoder to ViT-L. However, all multiprofile experiments so far have used concat fusion exclusively, leaving the fusion strategy as an untested design lever in the best-performing regime. Config_027 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted relative to config_020, providing a clean single-variable comparison. This is the most informative next step because: (1) it directly tests whether learned modality weighting can further improve on the current best, (2) it isolates the fusion effect without confounding changes to encoder, aggregation, or profile setting, and (3) the result will clarify whether further gains should be sought in fusion, RNA encoder (e.g., scgpt), or aggregation (e.g., transformer) under the ViT-L setting, guiding subsequent experiments efficiently under the limited budget.

The current best (config_020: scvi_n200, vit_l, avgpool, concat, acc 0.715) establishes a strong baseline. The largest remaining uncertainty is the RNA encoder choice: we have only tested pca_n2000 and scvi_n200, while scgpt is completely unexplored. config_021 changes exactly one variable from config_020 (RNA encoder scvi_n200 → scgpt) while holding the known-best image encoder (vit_l), aggregation (avgpool), fusion (concat), and profile setting (multiprofile) fixed. This isolates the effect of the RNA representation. Because scgpt is a generative single-cell model with a fundamentally different inductive bias than scvi, the prior uncertainty is high—it could substantially outperform or underperform scvi_n200. By contrast, the aggregation question (avgpool vs transformer) already has evidence favoring avgpool (config_003 vs config_014, ~4-pt gap), making a transformer test with vit_l lower expected information gain. Testing scgpt is therefore the highest-value single-variable experiment: it either confirms scvi_n200 as the preferred RNA encoder or reveals a new promising direction, directly reducing uncertainty about a core design axis under the limited budget.

The current best configuration (config_020: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) achieves 0.715 accuracy. The only untested single-variable modification in this neighborhood is aggregation: switching from avgpool to transformer (config_050 keeps all other settings identical). We have one prior data point suggesting avgpool > transformer (config_003 vs config_014 with pca+resnet50: 0.619 vs 0.579), but that was with weaker encoders. With the richer, higher-dimensional representations from ViT-L, transformer aggregation may better capture inter-profile interactions that simple averaging discards. This experiment directly tests whether the aggregation preference shifts with stronger image representations, isolates a single design decision, and either yields an improved configuration or confirms avgpool as optimal—making it the highest-value next step for exploiting the most promising region under a limited budget.

Evidence: The best-performing config is config_050 (scvi_n200, ViT-L, transformer, concat; 0.7207 acc), closely followed by config_020 (same but avgpool; 0.7150). We have two data points on fusion type with avgpool (concat 0.7150 vs weighted 0.7062), but no data on how fusion interacts with transformer aggregation. Question: Does weighted fusion complement or conflict with transformer aggregation in the scvi_n200 + ViT-L setting? This is a clean single-variable test (concat → weighted) holding all other factors at their best-known values. Why best next experiment: It directly extends the top-performing configuration to either find a new best or confirm concat is optimal, resolving the fusion question in the transformer regime with minimal confounding. Under a tight budget, isolating this one interaction is more informative than a broader exploration when the current best direction is already well-supported.
